title: Acute cholecystitis
scenario: A 43-year-old man presented with RUQ pain, nausea and vomiting. 439B · Archive
A patient presented to the ER with RUQ pain (discussion station). 430F

qs.q: Take a brief history.
a: Pain (SOCRATES): RUQ, colicky/constant, recurrent?, radiation to the right shoulder/back, aggravated by fatty food, relieved by NPO/vomiting/painkillers.

Associated: N/V, fever, chills; dark urine, pale stool, jaundice, itching (CBD stone/cholangitis). Risk factors: female, 40s, OCP, fatty diet, rapid weight loss, sickle-cell anaemia, bariatric surgery.
PMH (stones), drugs (NSAIDs), surgery, family history of stones, social (alcohol, travel/drugs — hepatitis).
qs.why: The history must characterise biliary pain (RUQ, after fatty meals, radiating to the shoulder), separate simple colic from inflammation (fever, constant pain) and from duct obstruction (jaundice, dark urine, pale stool), and list the "fat, female, forty" risk factors.
hist: RUQ pain, character, recurrence
Recurrent colicky RUQ pain is biliary colic; constant pain lasting longer suggests cholecystitis.
Radiation to right shoulder/back
Diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the right shoulder.
Fatty food aggravates, NPO/vomiting relieves
Fat stimulates CCK, which makes the gallbladder contract against an obstructing stone.
Nausea, vomiting, fever, chills
Fever shows inflammation/infection (cholecystitis rather than simple colic).
Dark urine, pale stool, jaundice, itching
Suggest a stone in the CBD (obstructive jaundice) or cholangitis, which changes management (needs ERCP).
Female, 40s, OCP, fatty diet, rapid weight loss
The classic risk factors for cholesterol stones.
Sickle-cell anaemia
Haemolysis produces pigment stones.
Bariatric surgery
Rapid weight loss after surgery causes stone formation.
PMH, drugs, family history, alcohol, travel
Previous stones, family tendency and risk factors for hepatitis help the differential.

qs.q: Examine the patient.
a: General appearance, vital signs, abdominal examination including Murphy's sign.
qs.why: Vitals show sepsis; the abdominal exam localises tenderness to the RUQ and tests Murphy's sign, the classic sign of an inflamed gallbladder.

qs.q: Explain what you mean by Murphy's sign.
a: Palpate the right subcostal area (mid-clavicular line) and ask the patient to take a deep breath and hold it; if inspiration stops (catches) because of pain as the inflamed gallbladder hits the hand → positive.
qs.why: On deep inspiration the inflamed gallbladder descends onto the examining hand and the pain stops the breath — a sign of gallbladder inflammation, not just stones.

qs.q: What is the differential diagnosis?
a: Biliary colic / cholelithiasis, acute cholecystitis, acute gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, acute pancreatitis.
qs.why: RUQ pain differentials are the biliary spectrum (colic → cholecystitis) and neighbouring organs: stomach/duodenum and pancreas.

qs.q: What type of imaging would you like to do?
a: Abdominal ultrasound.
qs.why: Ultrasound is cheap, radiation-free and the most sensitive test for gallstones and gallbladder inflammation.

qs.q: What will you look for in the US? / What are the possible findings?
a: Always comment on 3 things: stones (yes), gallbladder wall thickening (yes; normal < 3 mm), dilated biliary tree (no).
+ pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign.
qs.why: Stones + thick wall + pericholecystic fluid + sonographic Murphy = acute cholecystitis; a dilated duct would point to a CBD stone.

qs.q: How will you manage this patient in the ER?
a: Admit; NPO; 2 large-bore IV lines (14–16 G); bloods: CBC (leukocytosis), LFT, U&E, cross-match, coagulation profile, pancreatic enzymes.
IV fluids (e.g. 1 L NS / Ringer's lactate), analgesia (paracetamol 1 g) + antispasmodic, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin); monitor (BP, HR, SpO₂, urine output).
qs.why: Cholecystitis is an inflammatory/infective process — rest the gut, resuscitate, relieve pain and give antibiotics covering gut organisms, while bloods look for complications (pancreatitis, obstruction).

qs.q: What is the surgical management? (surgical window)
a: Within the window (≈ 48–72 h, depends on the surgeon's experience) → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Beyond the window → conservative (NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesia), then interval cholecystectomy ≈ 6 weeks–2 months later.
Getting worse despite treatment → operate; if unfit for anaesthesia → US/CT-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy, cholecystectomy when stable.
qs.why: Early cholecystectomy within the first days is easier before dense adhesions form and shortens stay; after the window, inflammation makes surgery dangerous so it is delayed ~6 weeks. A gallbladder drain (cholecystostomy) rescues the unfit.

qs.q: What are the complications of cholecystectomy?
a: CBD injury & bile leak, bleeding, infection, bowel perforation (duodenum/colon).
qs.why: The feared complication is bile duct injury (misidentifying the CBD as the cystic duct); bleeding, bile leak, infection and bowel injury from trocars/diathermy also occur.

tips.t: Doctor's advice: if asked for the exact time, say "48–72 hours, depending on the surgeon's experience" — not a fixed 48 h.

title: Head-of-pancreas cancer
scenario: Old patient with mild/vague upper abdominal pain and jaundice for 3 months. ("Mild/vague pain" = painless — Dr Al-Shaabi) 430A · 430F · Archive
A 75-year-old man presented with jaundice; a CT scan is shown. Old exam

imgs.cap: Contrast CT abdomen — hypodense mass in the head of the pancreas
Official answer sheet photographed in the 430 exam

qs.q: Mention three more focused questions in the history.
a: Dark urine, pale stool, itching, weight loss, loss of appetite; N/V, bowel habit.
Risk factors: male, old age, smoking, DM, chronic pancreatitis, alcohol.
qs.why: Ask for the features of obstruction (dark urine, pale stool, itching), of malignancy (weight loss, anorexia) and the risk factors — smoking is the most important.
hist: Dark urine, pale stool, itching
Confirm obstructive jaundice from a mass compressing the distal CBD.
Weight loss, loss of appetite
Constitutional symptoms suggest malignancy rather than a stone.
Nausea, vomiting
May indicate duodenal (gastric outlet) obstruction by the tumour.
Bowel habit
Pale, fatty stools (steatorrhoea) from exocrine failure.
Male, old age, smoking, DM, chronic pancreatitis, alcohol
Risk factors for pancreatic cancer; new-onset diabetes in an older patient can be an early sign.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, periampullary tumour, gallbladder tumour, CBD stone, cholangitis.
qs.why: Painless obstructive jaundice in the elderly is malignancy until proven otherwise — pancreatic head, ampulla, bile duct or gallbladder.

qs.q: What sign do you expect on examination?
a: Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice → unlikely to be gallstones.
qs.why: Courvoisier's law: a palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be stones (a stone-diseased gallbladder is fibrosed and can't distend) — think tumour.

qs.q: How would you investigate this patient?
a: Blood: CBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation profile, tumour marker CA 19-9.
Imaging: US abdomen (dilated biliary tree & gallbladder, pancreatic/liver masses) → contrast CT abdomen (mass in the head of pancreas, metastases, "double-duct sign").
qs.why: US confirms biliary obstruction; contrast CT stages the tumour (resectability, metastases); CA 19-9 supports the diagnosis and follow-up.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Pancreatic head cancer obstructing the CBD (obstructive jaundice).
qs.why: A pancreatic head mass compressing the distal CBD causes progressive painless obstructive jaundice.

qs.q: What do you see on the CT?
a: Axial contrast-enhanced CT abdomen showing a hypodense mass in the head of the pancreas.
qs.why: Name the modality and phase, then the finding: a hypodense mass in the pancreatic head (± double-duct sign).

qs.q: How would you treat this patient? (curative & palliative)
a: Resectable (no metastases): Whipple's procedure (or pylorus-preserving).
Unresectable / metastatic / unfit: palliation — ERCP + biliary stenting (or surgical bypass), then chemotherapy.
qs.why: Only resection (Whipple) offers cure; most patients are unresectable, and palliation aims to relieve jaundice (stent) and prolong life (chemotherapy).

qs.q: What is Whipple's procedure, how many anastomoses, and which is most important?
a: Pancreaticoduodenectomy: remove head of pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder and distal bile duct (± distal stomach).
3 anastomoses: pancreatico-jejunostomy, hepatico(choledocho)-jejunostomy, gastro/duodeno- jejunostomy.
Most important (most likely to leak): pancreatico-jejunostomy.
qs.why: Whipple removes the pancreatic head with duodenum, distal CBD and gallbladder, then restores continuity with three anastomoses; the soft pancreas makes the pancreaticojejunostomy the one that leaks.

qs.q: What types of stents are used in palliation, and when?
a: Metal: permanent (palliative), lasts 6–9 months.
Plastic: temporary / bridge to surgery; blocks within 4–6 weeks.
qs.why: Metal stents stay patent longer (for palliation); plastic stents block early and are used as a temporary bridge.

title: Acute cholangitis
seen_note: 436A — listed only; 438A — same as previous files ("initial and definitive management")
scenario: A patient presents with RUQ pain; positives on history were fever and jaundice. 437A

qs.q: Take a focused history.
a: Dark urine, pale stool, itching, jaundice, fever, chills, weight loss.
qs.why: Fever with rigors plus jaundice in a patient with biliary pain suggests infection behind an obstructed duct.
hist: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, itching
Confirm that the jaundice is obstructive (post-hepatic).
Fever, chills
With jaundice and RUQ pain they complete Charcot's triad — cholangitis.
Weight loss
Points to a malignant cause of the obstruction.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Acute (ascending) cholangitis — Charcot's triad: fever, RUQ pain, jaundice.
qs.why: Charcot's triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice) = cholangitis; with confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) it is life-threatening.

qs.q: What investigations will you do?
a: US and LFT (+ CBC, blood cultures, coagulation).
qs.why: LFTs show obstruction and US shows stones and duct dilatation; blood cultures and coagulation guide sepsis management.

qs.q: US shows an inflamed gallbladder and a dilated extrahepatic biliary system — what will you do?
a: MRCP.
qs.why: MRCP maps the ducts non-invasively and confirms a CBD stone before an intervention.

qs.q: What is the initial and definitive management?
a: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics, bloods.
ERCP (biliary decompression) followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission.
qs.why: Cholangitis is pus under pressure in the bile ducts — resuscitate and give antibiotics, then decompress the duct urgently by ERCP; remove the gallbladder in the same admission to prevent recurrence.

title: Acute gallstone (biliary) pancreatitis
scenario: A 45-year-old woman presented to the ER with epigastric pain for 8 hours. Archive
A case typical of biliary pancreatitis. 441A

imgs.cap: Abdominal X-ray showing gallstones (examiner shows this)

qs.q: Take a brief history.
a: Epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by leaning forward, aggravated by food; N/V; jaundice, pale stool, dark urine; bowel & urinary symptoms (rule out DDx).
Risk factors: alcohol, gallstones, drugs, hyperlipidaemia; previous ERCP; smoking, fatty diet.
qs.why: Typical pancreatic pain is epigastric, boring, through to the back and eased by leaning forward; the history must identify the cause (gallstones or alcohol) and exclude mimics.
hist: Epigastric pain → back, relieved leaning forward
The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so pain goes through to the back; sitting forward reduces stretch on it.
Aggravated by food, nausea, vomiting
Food stimulates pancreatic secretion; vomiting is very common in pancreatitis.
Jaundice, pale stool, dark urine
Suggest a stone still obstructing the CBD (gallstone pancreatitis).
Bowel and urinary symptoms
Help exclude differentials such as obstruction, perforation and renal colic.
Alcohol, gallstones
The two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis.
Drugs, hyperlipidaemia, previous ERCP
Other recognised causes (drugs, high triglycerides, post-ERCP).
Smoking, fatty diet
Additional risk factors.

qs.q: Examine the abdomen.
a: Epigastric tenderness with guarding; signs of haemorrhagic pancreatitis: Cullen's, Grey- Turner's, Fox's signs.
qs.why: Epigastric tenderness and guarding are expected; Cullen's and Grey-Turner's signs show retroperitoneal haemorrhage in severe disease.

qs.q: What is the differential diagnosis?
a: Acute cholecystitis, pancreatitis, PUD, renal stone, pyelonephritis, inferior MI, dissecting aortic aneurysm.
qs.why: Upper abdominal pain differentials include biliary and peptic disease, renal causes, and the vascular/cardiac emergencies that must not be missed.

qs.q: What investigations will you order, and why?
a: Labs: serum amylase & lipase; for Ranson: CBC (Hb, WBC), LDH, AST, glucose, U&E, Ca; lipid profile, LFT, coagulation.
CXR (pleural effusion, free air), AXR (sentinel loop, colon cut-off, calcification), US (gallstones → surgical; no stones → medical); CT not in all cases (necrosis/complications).
qs.why: Lipase/amylase > 3× normal confirm pancreatitis; the other bloods score severity; US looks for gallstones (which changes management); CT is for doubtful diagnosis or complications, not routine.

qs.q: How do you assess severity?
a: Ranson criteria, CRP, APACHE II.
qs.why: Ranson's criteria, CRP (> 150 at 48 h) and APACHE II predict severe disease and decide ward vs ICU care.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis? (examiner shows an X-ray with gallstones)
a: Gallstone (biliary) pancreatitis.
qs.why: Pancreatitis with gallstones on imaging = gallstone pancreatitis, the commonest cause.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: ABC, NPO, NGT, Foley, IV fluids, analgesia (pethidine), antibiotics if indicated; admit (ward/ICU); early enteral nutrition, then low-fat diet.
ERCP if there is cholangitis / obstructed CBD.
qs.why: Treatment is supportive: aggressive fluids, analgesia, early enteral feeding; ERCP only if a stone is obstructing the duct or there is cholangitis.

qs.q: What is the definitive management?
a: Cholecystectomy in the same admission (stone-related).
Infected necrosis (gas bubbles on CT) with systemic illness → necrosectomy.
qs.why: The stone source must be removed — cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild disease prevents another attack. Infected necrosis with systemic illness needs drainage/necrosectomy.

qs.q: What are the complications of acute pancreatitis?
a: Pleural effusion, ascites, bleeding, abscess, necrosis / walled-off necrosis, pseudocyst, jaundice, duodenal ileus.
qs.why: Local complications come from leakage and necrosis of pancreatic tissue (collections, pseudocyst, necrosis, bleeding); systemic ones from inflammation (effusions, ARDS, renal failure).

title: Obstructive jaundice — CBD stone (ERCP station)
scenario: A 45-year-old woman presented to the ER with RUQ pain, nausea and vomiting for 12 hours and jaundice. Archive Patient with abdominal pain and jaundice for 7 days; an ERCP picture is given. 435

imgs.cap: Labelled ERCP shown by Dr Al-Shaabi in the exam (scope, CBD, ERCP — dilated biliary tree with stones (filling defects) CHD, hepatic ducts, filling defect)
Obstructive jaundice (stones) vs head-of- pancreas cancer

qs.q: What further questions would you ask in the history?
a: Dark urine, pale stool, itching, fever/chills, weight loss.
qs.why: These questions confirm an obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice and look for its complications (cholangitis) and for malignancy (weight loss).
hist: Dark urine
Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is excreted in urine when bile flow is blocked.
Pale stool
No bilirubin reaches the gut, so stercobilin is missing.
Itching
Bile salts accumulate in the skin.
Fever, chills
Suggest cholangitis — infected obstructed bile, an emergency.
Weight loss
Raises suspicion of malignant obstruction (pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma) rather than a stone.

qs.q: What are the causes of CBD obstruction?
a: SINGE: Stricture, Iatrogenic, Neoplasm (head of pancreas/periampullary, cholangiocarcinoma), Gallstones, Extrinsic compression.
qs.why: SINGE covers the causes inside the duct (stones, stricture), in its wall (cholangiocarcinoma) and outside it (pancreatic head, nodes).

qs.q: What investigations will you do, and what do you want them to tell you?
a: LFT — obstructive picture: high total bilirubin (> 80 % direct), high ALP & GGT (no obstructive jaundice without high ALP); other labs (amylase, coagulation, WBC) normal.
US: gallstones, dilated biliary tree (CBD > 7 mm), gallbladder wall thickness.
qs.why: Conjugated bilirubin with high ALP/GGT confirms obstruction; ultrasound shows whether the ducts are dilated and whether stones are present.

qs.q: The US shows a dilated extrahepatic biliary system — how would you manage?
a: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, bloods → ERCP followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission.
If US is not conclusive, do EUS (or MRCP) — never ERCP just to diagnose (ERCP is therapeutic).
qs.why: A dilated duct with gallstones means a CBD stone: ERCP removes it and cholecystectomy in the same admission prevents recurrence. ERCP is therapeutic and risky, so diagnosis is by MRCP/EUS when unclear.

qs.q: What is the differential diagnosis?
a: CBD stone (obstructive jaundice), cholangitis, head-of-pancreas carcinoma, periampullary tumour, cholangiocarcinoma.
qs.why: Painful jaundice favours stones/cholangitis; painless jaundice favours tumours of the pancreatic head, ampulla or bile duct.

qs.q: Could it be a tumour of the head of the pancreas? Why?
a: Unlikely: the patient has pain (gallstones); pancreatic head cancer gives progressive painless jaundice.
qs.why: Pancreatic cancer classically gives progressive, painless jaundice (often with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder); colicky pain points to stones.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis from the history and picture?
a: CBD stone (choledocholithiasis).
qs.why: Acute pain plus obstructive jaundice and a filling defect in the duct = choledocholithiasis.

qs.q: What is the name of the modality in the picture?
a: ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography).
qs.why: The endoscope in the duodenum with contrast filling the biliary tree is the ERCP image.

qs.q: What structures do you see? Are there stones? Is the duct dilated?
a: Scope in the duodenum, contrast filling the CBD (common hepatic + cystic duct); filling defect = stone; duct dilated (compare its width with the scope, ~12–13 mm).
qs.why: Describe it systematically: the scope (for scale), the ducts filled, any filling defect (stone), and the duct diameter compared with the scope.

qs.q: Before doing the procedure, what do you have to do?
a: Consent; NPO; bloods incl. renal function (contrast), CBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation (correct any abnormality); US to confirm stones; prophylactic antibiotics.
qs.why: ERCP is invasive: consent, fasting, coagulation and renal function (contrast) are checked, and antibiotics given when the duct is obstructed.

qs.q: What are the complications of ERCP?
a: Acute pancreatitis, acute cholangitis, perforation, bleeding.
qs.why: Cannulating the papilla irritates the pancreas (pancreatitis — commonest), contrast in an obstructed duct seeds infection (cholangitis), and sphincterotomy can bleed or perforate.

qs.q: What are the complications of cholecystectomy?
a: CBD injury, bleeding, infection, bowel perforation (duodenum/colon), bile leak.
qs.why: Bile duct injury is the most serious complication; bleeding, infection, bile leak and bowel injury are the others.

qs.q: What is your management?
a: Remove the stone by ERCP and do cholecystectomy in the same admission.
qs.why: Clear the duct first (ERCP) and remove the source of stones (cholecystectomy) in the same admission — waiting risks recurrent pancreatitis or cholangitis.

qs.q: When do you put a stent?
a: Unsure the stones were completely cleared, cholangitis, or strictures.
qs.why: A stent keeps bile draining when the duct can't be fully cleared, when sepsis needs fast decompression, or when a stricture blocks it.

title: Pancreatic pseudocyst
scenario: A 52-year-old man, 6 weeks after severe biliary pancreatitis (cholecystectomy not done due to instability), presents with crampy abdominal pain, vomiting and obstipation; distended abdomen and tinkling bowel sounds (looks like small-bowel obstruction). (new case) 442A · 442B

imgs.cap: CT abdomen — large pseudocyst compressing the stomach

qs.q: Summarise the case.
a: A 52-year-old man, 6 weeks after severe biliary pancreatitis, now with crampy abdominal pain, vomiting and obstipation. (Gift question — just read the case aloud.)
qs.why: Summarising shows you picked out the key facts: recent severe pancreatitis plus new obstructive symptoms.

qs.q: What do you want to do next?
a: Vitals! + labs: CBC, U&E, coagulation profile, type & cross-match, LFT. (A paper of labs was handed — all normal.)
qs.why: Always check stability first, then bloods to look for sepsis, bleeding or organ dysfunction.

qs.q: Labs are normal — what next?
a: CT scan of the abdomen.
qs.why: CT shows pancreatic collections and what they compress — the cause of the obstruction here.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Pancreatic pseudocyst compressing the stomach.
qs.why: A well-defined fluid collection ≥ 4 weeks after pancreatitis is a pseudocyst; a large one can compress the stomach and cause outlet obstruction.

qs.q: What is the appropriate management?
a: Endoscopic (transgastric) drainage.
qs.why: A symptomatic mature pseudocyst abutting the stomach is drained endoscopically into the stomach (cystgastrostomy) — less invasive than surgery.

qs.q: What if it fails?
a: Surgical drainage.
qs.why: If endoscopy fails, surgical internal drainage (cystgastrostomy/cystjejunostomy) is the next step.

qs.q: Drainage was successful — what do you do next?
a: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy to prevent further attacks.
qs.why: The cause was gallstones — cholecystectomy prevents another attack of pancreatitis.

title: Hepatocellular carcinoma on cirrhosis
scenario: A 64-year-old man, known cirrhosis due to hepatitis C, referred after a 2 × 2 cm hepatic lesion on US. (new station) 438F

qs.q: What labs will you order?
a: LFT, hepatitis serology, tumour marker (AFP).
qs.why: LFTs assess liver reserve, serology confirms the cause, and AFP supports HCC.

qs.q: What imaging?
a: Triphasic (multiphase) CT.
qs.why: Multiphase CT shows the characteristic vascular behaviour of HCC, which is diagnostic in a cirrhotic liver.

qs.q: What are the findings on triphasic CT?
a: Arterial-phase enhancement with early (portal/delayed) wash-out.
qs.why: HCC is fed by the hepatic artery — it enhances in the arterial phase and washes out in portal/delayed phases.

qs.q: If the CT is atypical, what would you order?
a: MRI.
qs.why: MRI is more sensitive for small or atypical lesions.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: HCC on a background of hepatitis C cirrhosis.
qs.why: A new liver lesion with typical imaging in a cirrhotic patient (hepatitis C) is HCC.

qs.q: Which tumour marker?
a: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).
qs.why: AFP is the HCC tumour marker, used with imaging for diagnosis and follow-up.

qs.q: What is the ultimate treatment?
a: Liver transplant.
qs.why: Transplant removes both the tumour and the cirrhotic liver that would grow new tumours (within the Milan criteria).

qs.q: What other treatments are there?
a: Resection (if liver function allows), radiofrequency ablation, chemo-embolisation (TACE), systemic therapy (sorafenib).
qs.why: Choice depends on tumour size/number and liver function: resection or ablation for small tumours, TACE for intermediate disease, systemic therapy for advanced.

qs.q: Do you need a biopsy? Indications?
a: No — only if the diagnosis is unclear on imaging.
qs.why: Typical imaging in a cirrhotic liver is diagnostic; biopsy risks bleeding and tumour seeding, so it is reserved for atypical lesions.

title: Hepatic haemangioma
scenario: A 40-year-old patient with an upper abdominal mass and colicky pain for 6 months. 439F

imgs.cap: Triphasic CT — peripheral nodular enhancement with gradual centripetal fill-in

qs.q: Take a history.
a: Liver-mass history; the doctor concentrated on the OCP history.
qs.why: OCP use is linked to hepatic adenoma (and haemangioma growth), so it is the key history point for a liver mass in a young woman.
hist: Liver-mass history
Pain, fullness, weight loss and liver-disease risk factors help separate benign from malignant liver lesions.
OCP history
Oestrogen is linked to growth of haemangiomas and adenomas; this is why the doctor focused on it.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: HCC, hepatic haemangioma, hepatic cyst (also adenoma, FNH, metastasis).
qs.why: Benign lesions (haemangioma, cyst, FNH, adenoma) are commoner than HCC in a non-cirrhotic liver, but malignancy must be excluded.

qs.q: What investigation will you order?
a: Triphasic CT.
qs.why: Triphasic CT characterises liver lesions by their enhancement pattern.

qs.q: Describe the image.
a: Triphasic CT abdomen: peripheral (nodular) enhancement in the early arterial phase with gradual central (centripetal) filling.
qs.why: Haemangiomas fill from the periphery inward (peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in).

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Hepatic haemangioma.
qs.why: That enhancement pattern is diagnostic of haemangioma, the commonest benign liver tumour.

qs.q: What are the surgical indications?
a: Symptomatic (pain), increasing size with mass effect (stomach/duodenum), increasing destruction of liver; otherwise no treatment needed.
qs.why: Most haemangiomas are harmless and are left alone; surgery only for symptoms, growth with pressure effects, or uncertainty.
